questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Law of sines: side opposite a known angle
questions.stem: In triangle ABC, angle $A = 40^\circ$, angle $B = 65^\circ$, and side $a = 12\text{ m}$ (opposite angle A). Find side $b$ (opposite angle B).

variables.meaning: Sides opposite angles A and B

solution.title: Identify the matching pairs
solution.text: Side $a = 12\text{ m}$ is opposite $A = 40^\circ$; the unknown side $b$ is opposite $B = 65^\circ$.

solution.title: Write the law of sines
solution.text: Pair each side with the sine of its opposite angle.

solution.title: Solve for b
solution.text: Substitute the sine values.

questions.insight: The larger side is always opposite the larger angle: since $B > A$, $b$ must exceed 12 m, which immediately rules out 8.51 m.
commonErrors: Inverting the ratio, $12\sin 40^\circ/\sin 65^\circ = 8.51\text{ m}$.
Using angle $C = 75^\circ$ instead of $B$, which gives side $c = 18.03\text{ m}$.
Leaving the calculator in radian mode gives 13.32 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Law of cosines: third side of a triangular lot
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangular lot measure 25 m and 40 m, and the angle between them is $110^\circ$. Find the length of the third side.

solution.title: Choose the law
solution.text: Two sides and the included angle (SAS) call for the law of cosines.

solution.title: Evaluate the cosine term
solution.text: Since $\cos 110^\circ = -0.34202$, the last term becomes positive.

solution.title: Take the square root
solution.text: Solve for the third side.

questions.insight: With an obtuse included angle, the third side is longer than $\sqrt{a^2+b^2} = 47.17\text{ m}$, a quick reasonableness check.
commonErrors: Dropping the negative sign of $\cos 110^\circ$ gives 39.26 m.
Ignoring the angle and using the Pythagorean theorem gives 47.17 m.
Using $4ab\cos C$ instead of $2ab\cos C$ gives 59.94 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Height of a tower from two angles of elevation
questions.stem: From point P on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a tower is $32^\circ$. After walking 50 m directly toward the tower to point Q, the angle of elevation becomes $47^\circ$. Neglecting the height of the observer, find the height of the tower.
given: $PQ = 50\text{ m}$, Q between P and the tower

variables.meaning: Angles of elevation at P and Q

solution.title: Angles of triangle P-Q-Top
solution.text: The angle at Q inside the triangle is $180^\circ - 47^\circ = 133^\circ$, so the angle at the top equals the difference of the elevation angles.

solution.title: Slant distance from Q
solution.text: Apply the law of sines in triangle P-Q-Top.

solution.title: Height from the right triangle at Q
solution.text: The tower height is the vertical leg of the right triangle at Q.

solution.title: Check with the cotangent form
solution.text: The same result follows from the two-angle formula.

questions.insight: The angle subtended at the top (15 degrees) is small, so the result is sensitive to errors in the measured angles; a longer baseline improves accuracy.
commonErrors: Multiplying the slant distance Q-Top by $\sin 32^\circ$ instead of $\sin 47^\circ$ gives 54.25 m.
Stopping at the slant distance from Q (102.37 m) or the slant distance from P (141.29 m).

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Maximum area fenced on three sides along a river
questions.stem: A rectangular lot beside a straight river is to be fenced on three sides only; the side along the river needs no fence. If 240 m of fencing is available, what is the maximum area that can be enclosed?
given: Total fencing $= 240\text{ m}$ on three sides
Side along the river is unfenced

solution.title: Area in one variable
solution.text: Let $x$ be each side perpendicular to the river and $y$ the side parallel to it.

solution.title: Set the derivative to zero
solution.text: Differentiate and solve.

solution.title: Confirm and compute
solution.text: $A'' = -4 < 0$ confirms a maximum.

questions.insight: At the optimum the side parallel to the river is twice each perpendicular side: the free river boundary is used as fully as possible.
commonErrors: Fencing all four sides and taking a 60 m square gives 3600 m².
Assuming the three fenced sides are equal at 80 m each gives 6400 m².

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Open-top cylindrical tank of minimum sheet metal
questions.stem: An open-top cylindrical tank (bottom and side only) must hold $10\text{ m}^3$. Find the radius that minimizes the sheet metal used.
given: Open top: bottom and lateral surface only
questions.required: Radius $r$ that minimizes the surface area.

solution.title: Area in terms of r
solution.text: Eliminate $h$ using the volume constraint.

solution.title: Differentiate
solution.text: Set the first derivative to zero.

solution.title: Substitute
solution.text: Use $V = 10\text{ m}^3$.

solution.title: Confirm minimum
solution.text: $S'' = 2\pi + 4V/r^3 > 0$, so this is a minimum; the height also equals 1.471 m.

questions.insight: For an open-top cylinder of minimum material, the height equals the radius; with a top cover the optimum height equals the diameter.
commonErrors: Including a top cover gives $r = (V/2\pi)^{1/3} = 1.168\text{ m}$.
Reporting the diameter (2.942 m) instead of the radius.
Taking $r^2 = V/\pi$ (as if the height were 1 m) gives 1.784 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Binomial probability of defective hollow blocks
questions.stem: Five percent of the concrete hollow blocks from a supplier are defective. If 10 blocks are selected at random, what is the probability that exactly 2 are defective? Assume independent selections.

solution.title: Count the arrangements
solution.text: Number of ways to choose 2 defectives among 10 blocks.

solution.title: Apply the binomial formula
solution.text: Substitute $p = 0.05$ and $1 - p = 0.95$.

questions.insight: Even with only 5% defectives, there is roughly a 7.5% chance that a sample of 10 contains exactly two defective blocks.
commonErrors: Omitting $\binom{10}{2}$ gives 0.0017.
Computing at least 2 instead of exactly 2 gives 0.0861.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Differential leveling through one turning point
questions.stem: The elevation of BM-A is 125.430 m. A level run to BM-B records: BS on BM-A = 1.425 m, FS on TP-1 = 2.310 m, BS on TP-1 = 0.875 m, FS on BM-B = 1.940 m. Find the elevation of BM-B.
given: BS on BM-A $= 1.425\text{ m}$, FS on TP-1 $= 2.310\text{ m}$
BS on TP-1 $= 0.875\text{ m}$, FS on BM-B $= 1.940\text{ m}$

solution.title: First setup
solution.text: Height of instrument and elevation of TP-1.

solution.title: Second setup
solution.text: Backsight on TP-1, foresight on BM-B.

solution.title: Arithmetic check
solution.text: Starting elevation plus sum of BS minus sum of FS.

questions.insight: The sum of foresights exceeds the sum of backsights by 1.950 m, so BM-B lies 1.950 m below BM-A.
commonErrors: Subtracting backsights and adding foresights gives 127.380 m.
Adding every reading to the starting elevation gives 131.980 m.
Stopping at the turning point TP-1 gives 124.545 m.

questions.stem: A level sight is taken on a rod 1.5 km away. Using $h_{cr} = 0.0675K^2$ (m, with $K$ in km), what is the combined correction for Earth curvature and atmospheric refraction?

solution.title: Apply the combined formula
solution.text: Use $K$ in kilometers.

solution.title: Evaluate
solution.text: Compute the correction.

questions.insight: Over 1.5 km the line of sight departs from a level surface by about 15 cm, which is why balanced backsight and foresight distances are used in precise leveling.
commonErrors: Using the curvature coefficient 0.0785 alone gives 0.177 m.
Forgetting to square $K$ gives 0.101 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Departure of a traverse course
questions.stem: A traverse course has a bearing of N $35^\circ 20'$ E and a length of 120.50 m. What is its departure?
questions.required: Departure of the course, with sign (east positive).

solution.title: Convert the bearing angle
solution.text: Express minutes as a decimal of a degree.

solution.title: Departure
solution.text: Departure is the east-west component.

solution.title: Sign
solution.text: The bearing ends in E, so the departure is positive. (The latitude would be $120.50\cos 35.3333^\circ = +98.30\text{ m}$, north.)

questions.insight: Latitude uses the cosine and departure the sine of the bearing angle, because bearings are measured from the north-south meridian.
commonErrors: Using cosine gives the latitude, 98.30 m.
Evaluating the sine with the calculator in radian mode gives −84.39 m.
Assigning a negative sign to an easterly course gives −69.69 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Area of a four-sided lot by coordinates
questions.stem: The corners of a four-sided lot, taken in order, have coordinates (E, N) in meters: A (1000.00, 1000.00), B (1120.00, 1015.00), C (1150.00, 1095.00), D (1030.00, 1110.00). Find the area of the lot.

variables.meaning: Easting and northing of corner i

solution.title: Shift the origin
solution.text: Subtract 1000 from every coordinate; a translation does not change area.

solution.title: Cross products
solution.text: Compute $x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$ around the polygon, including the closing term D to A.

solution.title: Sum and halve
solution.text: Take half the absolute value of the sum.

questions.insight: Shifting the origin to one corner keeps the products small and reduces arithmetic slips without affecting the area.
commonErrors: Forgetting the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ gives 22,800 m².
Approximating with the averages of opposite sides, which is exact only for a rectangle, gives about 12,060 m².
Halving twice gives 5,700 m².

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Radius from the arc-basis degree of curve
questions.stem: A simple curve has a degree of curve of $4^\circ$ using the arc basis with a 20-m arc. What is its radius?

solution.title: Arc-basis relation
solution.text: On the arc basis, a 20-m arc subtends the angle D at the center.

solution.title: Substitute
solution.text: Use $D = 4^\circ$.

questions.insight: The chord basis, $R = 10/\sin(D/2) = 286.54\text{ m}$, differs by only 6 cm here; the two definitions diverge noticeably only for sharp curves.
commonErrors: Using the 100-ft arc constant 5729.58 gives 1432.39, which is in feet-based units, not meters.
Using a 10-m or 40-m arc by mistake gives 143.24 m or 572.96 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Stationing of the PT of a simple curve
questions.stem: A simple curve of radius 300 m connects two tangents that intersect at station 10+250.000 with an intersection angle of $36^\circ$. Find the station of the PT. (Choices give the station both as a running distance in meters and in station notation.)

solution.title: Tangent distance
solution.text: Distance from PI back to PC.

solution.title: Station of the PC
solution.text: Subtract T from the PI station.

solution.title: Length of curve
solution.text: Arc length from PC to PT.

solution.title: Station of the PT
solution.text: Stationing continues along the curve, so add the arc length to the PC station.

questions.insight: Stations are measured along the route, so the PT station is PC plus arc length, not PI plus tangent; the difference here is 6.456 m.
commonErrors: Taking Sta. PT = Sta. PI + T gives 10+347.476.
Adding the long chord instead of the arc length to the PC gives 10+337.934.
Adding half the curve length to the PI gives 10+344.248.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Highest point of an unequal-grade summit curve
questions.stem: A symmetrical parabolic summit curve 200 m long connects a $+3\%$ grade to a $-2\%$ grade. The PVI is at station 5+100 with elevation 150.00 m. Find the elevation of the highest point on the curve.
questions.required: Elevation of the highest point of the curve.

solution.title: PVC elevation
solution.text: The PVC is half the curve length before the PVI.

solution.title: Locate the high point
solution.text: The slope of the curve is zero at the high point.

solution.title: Elevation at the high point
solution.text: Substitute $x = 120\text{ m}$ into the parabola.

questions.finalAnswer: Elevation of high point $= 148.80\text{ m}$ at Sta. 5+120 (Choice A)
questions.insight: Because the back grade is steeper than the forward grade, the summit shifts past the PVI toward the PVT, 120 m from the PVC.
commonErrors: Assuming the high point is at the middle of the curve gives 148.75 m; that is only true for equal and opposite grades.
Taking the PVI elevation (150.00 m), which lies above the curve.
Reporting the PVT elevation (148.00 m).

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Stopping sight distance on a downgrade
questions.stem: Compute the stopping sight distance for a design speed of 90 km/h on a 4% downgrade. Use a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s, a coefficient of longitudinal friction of 0.30, and $SSD = 0.278Vt + V^2/[254(f \pm G)]$ with $V$ in km/h.

solution.title: Reaction distance
solution.text: The vehicle travels at full speed during the perception-reaction time.

solution.title: Braking distance
solution.text: On a downgrade gravity assists the motion, so the grade is subtracted from f.

solution.title: Total
solution.text: Add the two components.

questions.insight: A 4% downgrade lengthens the braking distance by about 15% compared with level ground, which matters on mountain highways.
commonErrors: Ignoring the grade gives 168.8 m.
Adding the grade as if it were an upgrade gives 156.3 m.
Leaving out the reaction distance gives 122.7 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Flow rate from density and space-mean speed
questions.stem: On a freeway lane, the observed density is 40 veh/km and the space-mean speed is 54 km/h. What is the flow rate?

solution.title: Apply the fundamental relation
solution.text: Use consistent units (veh/km times km/h).

solution.title: Optional check
solution.text: The average headway is 3600/2160 = 1.67 s, a reasonable freeway value.

questions.insight: The relation $q = kv_s$ holds only with space-mean speed; using time-mean speed overstates the flow.
commonErrors: Converting speed to m/s (15 m/s) while keeping density in veh/km gives 600.
Dividing speed by density instead of multiplying gives 1.35.
Slipping a decimal place gives 21,600.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: CPM total float of a non-critical activity
questions.stem: A project network has the following activities (duration in days; predecessors in parentheses): P = 4 (none), Q = 3 (none), R = 5 (P), S = 2 (Q), T = 4 (R and S). What is the total float of activity S?

solution.title: Forward pass
solution.text: P 0 to 4, Q 0 to 3, R 4 to 9, S 3 to 5, T starts at $\max(9, 5) = 9$ and finishes at 13. Project duration = 13 days.

solution.title: Backward pass for S
solution.text: The only successor of S is T, with $LS_T = 13 - 4 = 9$, so $LF_S = 9$.

solution.title: Total float
solution.text: Difference between late and early start.

questions.insight: Activity S can slip up to 4 days without delaying the 13-day project; the critical path is P-R-T.
commonErrors: Reporting the late start (7) or the early finish (5) of S instead of its float.
Assuming every activity that feeds the final activity is critical (0 days).

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Effect of an activity delay on project duration
questions.stem: A project network has these activities (duration in days; predecessors in parentheses): A = 3 (none), B = 5 (none), C = 4 (A), D = 6 (A), E = 2 (B and C), F = 4 (D and E). If activity B is delayed by 4 days and everything else proceeds as planned, what will the new project duration be?
given: E = 2 d (B, C), F = 4 d (D, E)

solution.title: Original forward pass
solution.text: A 0 to 3, B 0 to 5, C 3 to 7, D 3 to 9, E $\max(5,7) = 7$ to 9, F $\max(9,9) = 9$ to 13. Duration = 13 days; critical paths A-C-E-F and A-D-F.

solution.title: Float of B
solution.text: Successor E has $LS = 9 - 2 = 7$, so $LF_B = 7$.

solution.title: Forward pass with B = 9 days
solution.text: E starts at $\max(9, 7) = 9$ and finishes at 11; F starts at $\max(9, 11) = 11$.

solution.title: Check
solution.text: Project delay equals the delay minus the float.

questions.insight: B's 2 days of float absorb part of the delay; the remaining 2 days push the project, and B-E-F becomes the new critical path.
commonErrors: Adding the full delay to the original duration without using the float gives 17 days.
Assuming the delay is absorbed because B is not on the original critical path gives 13 days.
Taking the length of the original path B-E-F, 11 days, as the project duration.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Cement bags for footings and columns
questions.stem: A small structure has 4 isolated footings, each 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 0.40 m thick, and 4 columns, each 0.35 m × 0.35 m in section and 3.2 m high above the footing. For the concrete mix specified, use 9.0 bags of cement (40 kg) per cubic meter of concrete. How many bags of cement are required? Round up to the next whole bag.

solution.title: Footings
solution.text: Volume of the four footings.

solution.title: Columns
solution.text: Volume of the four columns.

solution.title: Cement
solution.text: Total volume times the cement factor, rounded up.

questions.insight: Material quantities are always rounded up to whole units; in practice a wastage allowance is added on top of the computed quantity.
commonErrors: Estimating only the footings (32.4, so 33 bags) or only the columns (14.1, so 15 bags).
Counting only one footing but all four columns, 0.900 + 1.568 = 2.468 m³ (23 bags).

questions.required: Sum $S_{12}$ of blocks laid in 12 days.

solution.title: Identify the progression

solution.title: Apply the sum formula
solution.text: Substitute into the AP sum.

solution.title: Compute
solution.text: Evaluate.

commonErrors: Using $n d$ instead of $(n-1)d$ gives 2,520.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Filling a tank with two pumps and an open drain
questions.stem: Pump A alone can fill an elevated water tank in 6 h and pump B alone can fill it in 9 h. A drain valve, if left open, can empty the full tank in 12 h. Starting with an empty tank, both pumps are switched on but the drain is accidentally left open. Assuming constant rates, how long will it take to fill the tank?

variables.meaning: Filling times of pumps A and B
Time to fill with all three operating

solution.title: Rates
solution.text: Express each device as a fraction of a tank per hour; the drain works against the pumps.

solution.title: Net rate
solution.text: Add the rates using the common denominator 36.

solution.title: Time
solution.text: Time is the reciprocal of the net rate.

questions.insight: The open drain costs about 1.5 h compared with the 3.6 h needed by the two pumps alone.
commonErrors: Ignoring the drain gives 3.60 h.
Adding the drain rate as if it also filled the tank gives 2.77 h.
Subtracting pump B's rate instead of the drain's, $1/(1/6 - 1/9 + 1/12)$, gives 7.20 h.

questions.subject: mste

questions.stem: A city in Mindanao has a population of 1.80 million and is growing at 2.1% per year, compounded annually. Assuming the growth rate stays constant, how many years will it take for the population to reach 2.50 million?

solution.title: Set up the growth equation
solution.text: Annual compounding gives a geometric progression.

solution.title: Take logarithms
solution.text: Isolate the exponent.

solution.title: Compute
solution.text: Evaluate the common logarithms.

questions.insight: Any logarithm base works as long as numerator and denominator use the same base; mixing bases is a common trap.
commonErrors: Dividing $\log(1.38889)$ by $r = 0.021$ instead of by $\log 1.021$ gives 6.79 years.
Assuming linear (simple) growth gives 18.52 years.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Width of a slab from its area (quadratic equation)
questions.stem: A rectangular floor slab has an area of $180\text{ m}^2$. Its length is 3 m more than twice its width. Find the width of the slab.

solution.title: Form the equation
solution.text: Area equals width times length.

solution.title: Take the positive root
solution.text: A width must be positive.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Cross-sectional area of a regular octagonal column
questions.stem: A decorative column has a regular octagonal cross-section with each side measuring 0.25 m. Find the cross-sectional area of the column.

solution.title: Apothem
solution.text: Each of the 8 isosceles triangles has a half-angle of $180^\circ/8 = 22.5^\circ$ at the center.

solution.title: Perimeter
solution.text: Eight equal sides.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Great-circle distance from Manila to Tokyo
questions.stem: Take Manila at latitude 14.60° N, longitude 120.98° E and Tokyo at latitude 35.68° N, longitude 139.69° E. Treating the Earth as a sphere of radius 6371 km, find the great-circle distance between the two cities.

formulas.label: Spherical law of cosines for sides

solution.title: Spherical triangle
solution.text: Use the triangle formed by the North Pole and the two cities. The sides from the pole are the colatitudes, and the angle at the pole is the longitude difference.

solution.title: Law of cosines for sides
solution.text: Colatitude form rewritten with latitudes.

solution.title: Evaluate
solution.text: Substitute the trigonometric values.

solution.title: Central angle
solution.text: Take the inverse cosine.

solution.title: Distance
solution.text: Multiply the central angle in radians by the radius.

questions.insight: Over long distances the plane approximation fails because meridians converge toward the poles; the great circle is the shortest path on the sphere.
commonErrors: Treating degrees of latitude and longitude as a flat grid at 111.19 km per degree gives 3,134 km.
Interchanging sines and cosines of the latitudes (using colatitudes incorrectly) gives 2,478 km.
Solving the triangle with the plane law of cosines on the colatitudes gives 3,293 km.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Distance from a control point to a boundary line
questions.stem: On a local grid (in meters), a property boundary follows the line $5x + 12y - 20 = 0$. Find the perpendicular distance from control point P(7, 4) to the boundary line.
questions.required: Perpendicular distance $d$ from P to the line.

variables.meaning: Coefficients of the line Ax + By + C = 0

solution.title: Identify the coefficients

solution.title: Numerator
solution.text: Substitute the point into the left side of the line equation.

solution.title: Denominator and distance

questions.insight: The denominator normalizes the line's coefficients; 5-12-13 is a Pythagorean triple, so it comes out exact here.
commonErrors: Dividing by $A + B = 17$ instead of $\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ gives 3.71 m.
Dividing by $A^2 + B^2 = 169$ gives 0.373 m.
Dropping the constant term C gives 6.38 m.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Area between a parabola and a line
questions.stem: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola $y = 6x - x^2$ and the line $y = x$.

solution.title: Intersections

questions.subject: mste

solution.title: Temperature change
solution.text: The tape is warmer than standard, so it is longer than its nominal length.

solution.title: Apply the formula to the whole line
solution.text: Use the total measured length, not one tape length.

solution.text: A tape that is too long reads too short, so the correction is added.

questions.subject: mste
questions.title: Combined temperature, pull and sag corrections
questions.stem: A 30.000-m steel tape is of standard length at 20°C under a 50-N pull when fully supported. It is used to measure a line recorded as 360.000 m (exactly 12 full tape lengths), with the tape supported only at its ends, at a temperature of 31°C and a pull of 90 N. The tape has a cross-sectional area of 3.0 mm², $E = 200\text{ GPa}$, $\alpha = 11.6 \times 10^{-6}$ per °C, and a weight of 0.30 N/m. Find the total correction to the recorded length.
questions.required: Total correction to the recorded 360.000 m.

solution.title: Temperature correction per tape length
solution.text: Tape is warmer than standard, so it is longer.

solution.title: Pull correction per tape length
solution.text: Use $A = 3.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$ and $E = 200 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}$.

solution.title: Sag correction per tape length
solution.text: Sag always shortens the horizontal span, so it is negative.

solution.title: Net per tape length
solution.text: Add the three corrections.

solution.title: Total for 12 tape lengths
solution.text: Multiply by the number of tape lengths.

questions.finalAnswer: Total correction $= -0.0801\text{ m}$, so the true length is 359.920 m (Choice A)
questions.insight: Sag dominates here; raising the pull to the normal tension (where pull and sag corrections cancel) would remove most of the error.
commonErrors: Ignoring the sag correction gives +0.0699 m.
Applying only the sag correction gives −0.1500 m.
Treating the pull correction as negative gives −0.1281 m.

Setup near A: A = 1.402 m, B = 0.920 m
questions.required: Correct rod reading on B from the second setup.

variables.meaning: Readings from the setup near A

solution.text: Equal sight distances cancel the collimation error.

solution.title: Correct reading on B
solution.text: From the second setup, a horizontal line passing through reading 1.402 on A must hit B 0.436 m lower on the rod.

solution.title: Interpret the error
solution.text: The observed 0.920 m is 0.046 m too low, so the line of sight is inclined downward.

questions.insight: Balancing backsight and foresight distances cancels collimation error, which is why the midway setup gives the true difference in elevation.
